title: Remember a Soldier
sub: Grades 3–4 · The Memorial · Reading a memorial card
objective: Students will read memorial cards from *The Memorial*, each drawn from a real record of the American Battle Monuments Commission, and learn what a card can tell: a name, a rank, a state, a date and a resting place. They will meet a soldier, an Army nurse, a name on the Tablets of the Missing and a soldier *known but to God*, and learn how November 11 became Armistice Day and then Veterans Day.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every card is one real person. Reading it slowly, and keeping a silence, is how a whole country keeps a promise: you will not be forgotten.

items.text: read a memorial card: who the person was, where they came from, when they died and where they rest

connection: **Online,** *The Memorial*’s *Remember a soldier* draws a card for one of the fallen; search by name or by your own state, and print a card to keep. **In the exhibition,** take a soldier card from the display, and find the poppies and the date in red on the *When the Guns Fell Silent* poster.

steps.title: One small card
script: Show Adolph Kehrli’s card on page 3. Read it aloud slowly. *“What can you learn about this person from one small card?”* Take answers: his name, that he was a private, that he came from New York, the date. Then: *“What does the card not tell us?”* (His age, his family, what he was like.) *“At the Mini Museum, visitors took a card like this home, for one American who died in the Great War. Today we read them carefully.”*

screen.text:
In Memory
Adolph Kehrli
Private · 148th Infantry Regiment, 37th Division
From New York
Died October 31, 1918
Rests in: Flanders Field American Cemetery

steps.purpose: Meet one real person through a card, before any explanation.
students: What can you learn about this person from one small card?

steps.title: Four cards
script: **Four cards.** Show all four. Every card comes from the records of the American Battle Monuments Commission, which keeps the records of Americans who rest in its cemeteries overseas or are named on its Tablets of the Missing. Point out that Alice A. Ireland was a **nurse**: not everyone who served was a soldier. Adolf F. Klement, from Texas, was *Missing in Action*: he has no known grave, so his name is carved on the Tablets of the Missing.

screen.caption: Four cards from The Memorial, from the records of the American Battle Monuments Commission

steps.purpose: Compare four cards: who served, and the different ways they are remembered.
students: Who on these cards was not a soldier?
Which card has no name? Which has no grave?

steps.title: Known but to God
script: **Known but to God.** The fourth card has no name at all. Read its words. Some soldiers could never be identified. Their graves say they are *known but to God*. At Arlington National Cemetery, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier honors all those whose names we’ll never know; on Veterans Day, by tradition, the President places a wreath there.

screen.text:
Here rests in honored glory
an American soldier
known but to God
screen.cite: The Memorial’s card for an unknown soldier

steps.purpose: Understand the soldiers whose names we will never know.
students: What does this card not have?
Why might a soldier have no name on his grave?

steps.title: From Armistice Day to Veterans Day
script: **November 11.** Walk through the chart: the guns stopped at 11:00 AM on November 11, 1918. In 1919 President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed it *Armistice Day*, and Americans paused for two minutes at 11:00. In 1954 Congress renamed it *Veterans Day*, to honor all American veterans. Canada, Britain and France still call it *Remembrance Day*.

screen.caption: From Armistice Day to Veterans Day, as the When the Guns Fell Silent poster tells it

cells: At 11:00 AM on November 11, the armistice, the peace agreement, takes effect. The guns stop.
President Woodrow Wilson proclaims November 11 Armistice Day. At 11:00 AM, Americans pause for two minutes to honor the fallen.
Congress changes the name to Veterans Day, to honor all American veterans, not just those from World War I.
Canada, Britain and France still call it Remembrance Day, and keep two minutes’ silence at the eleventh hour.

steps.purpose: Follow November 11 from the end of the war to today.
students: Why was the name changed in 1954?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels read the Memorial’s cards and put the story of November 11 in order.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read one card and fill in its facts. Find what the unknown soldier’s card does and does not say. Number the story of November 11 in order and finish a sentence.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare three cards: a soldier, a nurse and a name on the Tablets of the Missing. Explain what *Missing in Action* means for a grave. Explain why Armistice Day became Veterans Day.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Read the unknown soldier’s card beside the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Sort what a card can and cannot tell. Compare Veterans Day and Remembrance Day, then write an inscription.

steps.purpose: Read real cards closely, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read cards from The Memorial and follow November 11 to Veterans Day.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back from the screen: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. For the last, ask a Red Level student to read their inscription.

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.

steps.title: The silence
script: Open *The Memorial* and choose *The silence at 11:00*. Say: *“Every year at 11 o’clock on November 11, people stop for two minutes to remember. Let’s keep the silence now, for Adolph, for Alice, for Adolf, and for the soldier known but to God.”* Press *Keep two minutes’ silence now*. Afterward, ask one student to read the poster’s promise: *“You will not be forgotten.”*

screen.cite: When the Guns Fell Silent at the 11th Hour

steps.purpose: Keep the two minutes’ silence together, as people do on November 11.
students: Think of the four people on the cards.
